summary: Gives requirements on IPng from the perspective of the Unified Routing Architecture described in RFC 1322. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo lists six routing requirements for IPng from the perspective of the Unified Routing Architecture. It covers flexible addressing hierarchies, forwarding, routing labels, and source routes.

questions: what routing requirements did rfc 1668 propose for ipng
subtitle: Routing and addressing requirements proposed for IPng.

tldr.problem: The IPng design needed routing requirements that support scalability without locking every part of the network into one hierarchy.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists six requirements for address assignment, forwarding information, routing labels, and source routing from the Unified Routing Architecture perspective.
tldr.outcome: It submits one set of IPng requirements to the IPng area and explicitly says publication does not imply that the ideas were accepted.

today: RFC 1668 is Informational. It records routing requirements submitted to the IPng area and does not imply that the area accepted them.

sections.title: Addressing and Forwarding Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 1668 responds to RFC 1550 with requirements for IPng from the perspective of the Unified Routing Architecture in RFC 1322. Addresses should support topologically significant assignment, while allowing different parts of the hierarchy to have different numbers of levels.

The packet header should carry enough information for a router to determine the next hop. Hierarchical address assignment should still allow both hierarchical and non-hierarchical routing.
sections.plainLanguage: IPng addresses should help routers scale, but they should not force every region to use the same hierarchy. Packets should also provide enough information for forwarding.

sections.title: Routing Labels and Source Routes
sections.content:
The memo says an IPng header should support a routing label or route ID that identifies a forwarding information base (FIB). It proposes strong and weak labels: if a router lacks a FIB for a strong label, it discards the packet and sends an error; with a weak label, it uses the default FIB and indicates that the requested label was unavailable.

Source routing should be able to name individual routers or collections, express when consecutive route entities must share a subnet, specify what to do if the next route entry is unavailable, and verify route feasibility.
sections.plainLanguage: A routing label can select which forwarding table a router uses. Source routes also need rules for unavailable paths and a way to check whether a route can work.

sections.title: Status of These Requirements
sections.content: The memo was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550. It states that publication does not imply acceptance of any ideas in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: This is one set of proposed requirements for IPng. Publishing it does not mean the IPng area accepted them.

references.text: Estrin, D., "Unified Routing Architecture", RFC 1322, May 1992.
RFC 1550, IPng solicitation referenced in this memo.
